newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler says Mitsubishi extension would be same.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler says Mitsubishi extension would be same.

text.p: The president of Chrysler Corp said Wednesday if the automaker extends its car production agreement with Mitsubishi Motors Corp, it would mirror the two automakers' current arrangement.

"If (an extension) is successfully consummated, it would merely be a continuation of the current deal we have," Robert A. Lutz said. "(Under that deal) we buy from them at a given price two coupe models, the (Dodge) Avenger and the (Chrysler) Sebring."
Lutz, 64, was in Pittsburgh on Wednesday to receive the annual Executive of the Year award from Carnegie Mellon University's Graduate School of Industrial Administration.
Chrysler said Monday it was exploring the possibility of extending its production agreement with Mitsubishi at an assembly plant in Normal, Ill.

The current agreement is set to expire after the 1999 model year. Mitsubishi Motor Manufacturing of America Inc, the U.S. arm of Mitsubishi Motors Corp, currently builds the Avenger, the Sebring and the Eagle Talon coupes at the plant.

"What discussions are focusing on now is does the relationship end with the expiration of the current models that we get from that plant, or would we renew for the next generation of vehicles," Lutz said. "These are important cars for us but not vital cars."

Separately, Lutz, who will become Chrysler's vice chairman on January 1 and is expected to stay at the automaker for another two years, said his role for his remaining tenure will be to keep the creative ball rolling.
"I want to continue to furnish creative inputs and have the ideas, and work together very closely with the product creation people to make sure that the creative process is alive and well," he said.
Robert Eaton, Chrysler's chairman and chief executive officer, will take on the additional title of president after Lutz assumes his new title.
Lutz has been credited with bringing a flair for product creativity to Chrysler and pushing through production of niche vehicles that are favorites with car enthusiasts, such as the Viper.

"I want to continue to make a major contribution, but not actually in physically doing things," Lutz said. He said he hopes to continue to move the mentality at Chrysler further toward what he called "right-brain creativity."

"(By that I mean) running the business more artistically and less by the numbers," he said. "That's worked very well for us...it makes (Chrysler) more profitable and a lot more fun to work. Together with our chairman I'd like to keep that process moving along until it becomes irreversible."
